extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, research integrity officers, principal investigators, institutional administrators, funders, and research integrity community
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for detecting, handling, and preventing image manipulation in biomedical research articles, aimed at stakeholders across the publication lifecycle (researchers, institutions, publishers, funders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic pre-publication image screening
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should examine all figure files of all accepted manuscripts for evidence of manipulation before publication (JCB instituted systematic screening).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement systematic screening in production workflows despite personnel costs; screening before publication prevents manipulated images from entering the literature. JCB used this approach starting in 2002 and trained other publishers. Screening can be done by staff and should be part of publisher responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual inspection using image adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual inspection of each image panel using adjustments (brightness/contrast) to enhance background and reveal inconsistencies (e.g., sharp lines, matching spot patterns) that indicate splicing or duplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Photoshop or similar tools to adjust contrast/brightness to detect clues like sharp lines around bands (copy/paste) or repeating background patterns (duplication). Visual inspection is the method used historically and remains critical—it's the gold standard for evaluating specific allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithms for large-scale screening (use at scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use algorithmic tools to screen submissions at scale against databases of previously published images (e.g., ImageTwin) to detect duplications across the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithms enable screening millions of images and make publisher/institution-wide screening feasible. They are recommended for scale and to identify candidate problems, but their outputs require human confirmation. Collaborative publisher-level screening against other publishers' submissions is a promising application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithms are not sufficient to adjudicate specific allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithmic outputs (positive or negative) are not proof for or against manipulation; algorithms are inappropriate as the sole evaluator of specific allegations (except possibly in generative-AI detection contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithms currently have too many false negatives and false positives for adjudicating particular cases—visual inspection by a trained human should confirm algorithm findings. Examples exist where algorithmic dismissal led to incorrect conclusions. A negative algorithm result is not proof of innocence; a positive result is not proof of guilt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human confirmation of algorithmic findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Any algorithmic detection must be evaluated and confirmed by a trained and knowledgeable human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithms can flag candidates, but a human should visually inspect images to confirm splicing, copy/paste, erasure, or duplication. Training non-scientific staff in visual screening and tool use is feasible and acceptable; reliance solely on algorithmic judgement is dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder-shared responsibility (Swiss cheese model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple stakeholders should screen data at different stages—funders (grant review), researchers/institutions (before submission), and publishers (during manuscript review/production)—so overlapping checks reduce failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt layered defenses acknowledging that each stage has holes; more stages close more holes. For example, funders could screen cited publications, institutions should screen manuscripts prior to submission, and publishers should screen accepted manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal investigator (PI) responsibility to check source data
rubrics_metrics.description: PIs must closely examine image data prepared for manuscripts from their labs before submission, comparing prepared figures to the underlying source data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PIs can delegate to trusted/trained lab members or core facilities, but the responsibility should be explicit and codified in institutional policy. The comparison is a side-by-side verification: 'do the data in the prepared figure match what was actually observed?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and importance of source data
rubrics_metrics.description: Source data are the original, unaltered files obtained through the research process (proprietary imaging system files or original X‑ray film), not the composed/assembled display (e.g., PowerPoint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that some acquisition software may alter images pre-save; in such cases, metadata should record alterations. Source data (and metadata) are required to dispel accusations; comparisons must be to these original files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandate perpetual retention of source data
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions should require retention of the data underlying published articles in perpetuity (or at least for the published figures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disk storage is now inexpensive; institutions should provide storage and structure. Springer Nature recommends retaining unprocessed data 'ideally in perpetuity'—the author argues this should be a requirement, not a recommendation, to aid investigations and prevent retractions due to missing data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proactive institutional screening and response
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions must shift from reactive handling of allegations (e.g., via PubPeer notifications) to proactive screening to prevent manipulated images being submitted and to monitor staff publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions could offer algorithmic screening as a service rather than relying solely on PIs to run tools. Subscribing to dashboards (e.g., PubPeer Dashboard) is useful but reactive; a proactive stance includes routine screening of staff outputs and publications of job candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dismiss anonymous allegations out of hand
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should not automatically disregard allegations from anonymous whistleblowers; anonymous post-publication peer review (e.g., PubPeer) has produced valid and important findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early dismissal of anonymous reports (e.g., from Clare Francis) hindered progress; courts have upheld commenters' right to anonymity. Treat allegations on their merits and investigate when evidence suggests potential misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention/use of metadata to detect pre-acquisition or pre-save alterations
rubrics_metrics.description: When images might have been altered before being saved in proprietary file types, file metadata should be examined as evidence of changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If alterations occurred at acquisition or within the acquisition software, traces should exist in metadata; investigators should inspect metadata as part of source-data comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of loading controls in blot experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Loading controls are essential; claims that a problematic image is 'just a loading control' are not acceptable because without a valid loading control the experiment cannot be interpreted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistencies (e.g., one blot panel spliced while loading control is not) indicate invalid comparisons. Invalid loading controls render conclusions unreliable and should be treated seriously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers should retain visual screening even when using algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers who introduce algorithmic screening should continue visual screening rather than downgrade to algorithm-only processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithms are useful as an additional check, especially for scale, but visual screening detects manipulation types that algorithms miss (e.g., splicing, erasure). Continue both methods where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and validation of detection algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Software developers must provide transparency about algorithm effectiveness (sensitivity/specificity) and independent validation so users understand capabilities and limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author calls for transparency from vendors; users need independent verification of performance, and institutions/publishers should validate tools before reliance. Lack of transparency can lead to misuse or overconfidence in algorithmic outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm strengths and limitations by image type
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms are reasonably good at detecting duplications in micrograph images but have limited effectiveness for blot images and for manipulations like copy/paste, erasure, or splicing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize per-image-type performance differences; do not generalize algorithm success from one image class (micrographs) to others (blots). Use algorithms accordingly and confirm findings visually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require source data provision to resolve allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: The sure way to dispel an allegation of image manipulation is for the accused researcher to provide the source data for comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to provide source data—sometimes due to short institutional retention policies—has led to retractions. Institutions should mandate retention, and investigators should request original files during probes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screen for paper-mill hallmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should use software to detect hallmarks of paper mill production and screen submissions for indicators of fabricated or mass-produced papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies found substantial fractions (e.g., 10–13%) of submissions to a major publisher bore paper-mill hallmarks. Screening for these patterns is part of integrity protection and should be implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funders should screen cited publications in grant applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Funders could dis-incentivize image manipulation by screening the publications applicants cite in grant proposals and progress reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screening by funders would reduce the chance of funding work built on fraudulent data; as of the article, this is a missed opportunity. Congressional admonishments to NIH to look for fraud could be operationalized via such screening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for generative AI as a new threat and detection need
rubrics_metrics.description: Generative AI can produce synthetic biomedical images (e.g., Western blots) that are difficult or impossible to detect visually, creating a new front requiring specialized detection algorithms and validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track research on GAN-generated blots and detectors; invest in validating detectors for AI-generated images, commercializing them, and implementing their use among stakeholders. Recognize an arms race: detectors must be independently validated and deployed quickly after development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and staffing for screening
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-scientific staff (e.g., copyeditors, proofreaders) can be trained in visual screening techniques and algorithm use to expand screening capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no work-arounds: images should be systematically screened before submission and during manuscript review. Training requirements are not onerous—teach visual techniques and tool operation; consider which stages are suitable for less-intensive screening by non-experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-benefit: screening personnel costs justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Although there are personnel costs to screen images, these costs are worth protecting the scientific record and saving time, reputation, and money from dealing with allegations later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the downstream savings from preventing manipulated data entering the literature; algorithms reduce per-item cost at scale but do not eliminate the need for human oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public awareness and reputational incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Public allegations (via PubPeer and media) increase awareness and create reputational incentives for stakeholders to take action on image integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency and public scrutiny make journals/institutions more likely to act; the rise of image sleuths has pressured stakeholders to implement screening and data-retention policies.
